newsitem.title: USA: March wholesale prices fall but some pressures showing.
newsitem.headline: March wholesale prices fall but some pressures showing.

text.p: Tumbling energy costs kept wholesale inflation in check during March, the government said Friday, although a strengthening economy and underlying price pressures seemed to suggest the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates again in the near future.
The Labour Department said the Producer Price Index fell 0.1 percent. But the underlying rate, which excludes often-volatile food and energy costs, rose an unexpected 0.4 precent.

At the same time, the Commerce Department said consumers slowed their buying spree last month, although strong upward revisions in retail sales for January and February caused analysts to reconsider just how strong the first quarter was.
"I was looking for growth of 3.5 to 4.0 percent in the first quarter, but now I think it may be more like 4.0 to 4.5 percent," said David Jones of Aubrey G. Lanston and Co.

Indications that economic growth accelerated from the 3.8 percent pace in the final three months of 1996 and that underlying inflation was showing unwanted vitality seemed a likely prescription for the Federal Reserve to push interest rates higher again.

"An accumulation of hard evidence -- subtle wholesale price pressures and strong retail sales -- will provide cover for another Fed-led rise in short-term interest rates," said Key Corp. Chief Economist Ken Mayland.
Federal Reserve policy-makers are scheduled to meet May 20 to discuss interest rates. They increased short-term rates by a quarter of a percentage point on March 25.
Retail sales rose last month by 0.2 percent to a seasonally adjusted $215.6 billion after revised upwardly increases of 1.5 percent in February and 1.7 percent in January.
An unexpected drop in sales by auto dealers -- after their strongest sales gain in a year during February -- held down overall sales in March, the Commerce Department said.

The March retail sales gain was weaker than anticipated by Wall Street economists, who had forecast a more robust 0.6 percent pickup in business. Some analysts, however, raised the possibility that this figure also could be revised upward.

"I think it confirms that consumer spending was strong in the first quarter," said David Sloan, an economist at I.D.E.A. Inc. "There is some possibility that spending will slow, but this data confirms a strong first quarter,

On the surface at least, it did not appear that producer prices, which have fallen for three months in a row, showed anything but benign inflationary pressures. They fell 0.4 percent in February and 0.3 percent percent in January.
The department said the drop in energy prices, which fell 3.4 percent after dropping 1.2 percent in February, was the largest decline in six years and reflected a warmer-than-expected winter.
Gasoline prices tumbled 4.0 percent after retreating 3.1 percent in February, while home heating oil plummeted 9.9 percent after falling 1.1 percent in the prior month.
With the often-volatile food and energy sector excluded, however, the picture was more threatening
This so-called core rate, which economists believe more closely tracks inflation than the overall figure, rose 0.4 percent after falling 0.1 percent in February.
Wall Street had estimated that overall prices would be unchanged, while the core rate would be up 0.1 percent.
"There might be some more inflation in the pipeline than what we had thought," said Astrid Adolfson of MCM Moneywatch Inc.

While energy prices were in retreat, food prices were going the other way in March, rising 0.9 percent after falling 0.3 percent in February. The department said the increase reflected a rise in beef, fish and vegetables prices.
Goods at the intermediate level of production, which require additional processing, fell 0.6 percent while so-called crude goods at the early level of production fell 6.9 percent.
It was the first time wholesale prices fell three months in a row since consecutive declines in May through August 1993.
